slides.text: Pt. Sharma informed Gandhi about the Kandel Satyagraha and accompanied him to Raipur. By this time, Gandhi's personality had already had an impact on the British. The mere announcement of his visit had won the Satyagraha before he arrived.
slides.visualDescription: Title card: Pt. Sundarlal Sharma speaking to Gandhi in a lamplit train compartment. Night outside the window. Two profiles — the architect of Chhattisgarh's awakening and the leader of India's freedom. A meeting that changes everything. Ink illustration.

slides.text: Calcutta, December 2, 1920. The city buzzes with Congress energy. The Nagpur session is weeks away. Leaders from across India are converging, travelling, organising. Among them: Pt. Sundarlal Sharma, arriving from Chhattisgarh with a specific mission.
slides.visualDescription: Calcutta, December 1920 — a busy colonial city on the eve of the Nagpur Congress. Railway station filled with political leaders from across India. Pt. Sundarlal Sharma — travel-worn, determined — arriving with one purpose: to find Gandhi.

slides.text: Gandhi was about to come from Calcutta to Nagpur. He would be passing through — and Chhattisgarh lay directly on the route. The logic was simple: if Gandhi was coming this far, a brief detour through Raipur would change Chhattisgarh forever.
slides.visualDescription: A railway map showing the Calcutta-Nagpur route. Raipur visible between them — just slightly off the main line but close enough. Sharma's finger tracing the route. The geography of opportunity. A brief detour with century-long consequences.

slides.text: Sharma found Gandhi and told him about the Kandel Canal Satyagraha — the false tax, the farmers' courage, the British concession. Gandhi listened with the attention he always gave to local struggles. He agreed to stop at Raipur.
slides.visualDescription: The meeting in Calcutta — Sharma standing before Gandhi, telling the story of Kandel with quiet intensity. Gandhi seated, listening completely. No aides, no ceremony. Two men and a story that would become history. The moment of agreement.

slides.text: Gandhi was accompanied on this journey by the Ali brothers — Maulana Shaukat Ali and Muhammad Ali — the towering leaders of the Khilafat Movement. Their joint travel symbolised the unity of the Khilafat and Non-Cooperation movements.
slides.visualDescription: The train from Calcutta: Gandhi, Shaukat Ali, Muhammad Ali seated together in a compartment. Three leaders of different backgrounds traveling toward the same destination — Nagpur, and now Raipur. The Khilafat and Non-Cooperation united in one journey.

slides.text: Sharma accompanied Gandhi on the train from Calcutta. Through the night, through the forests of the Central Provinces, toward Chhattisgarh. Sharma carried in his memory every name, every story, every village that was waiting. He was the bridge.
slides.visualDescription: The night train crossing into Chhattisgarh. Through the window: Sal forest, stars, the occasional lamp of a village. Sharma awake, looking out the window with the expression of a man bringing something precious home. Gandhi asleep beside him.

slides.text: In Raipur, preparations were complete. Pt. Ravi Shankar Shukla, Thakur Pyarelal Singh, Sakharam Dubey — the leaders of Chhattisgarh's Congress movement — waited on the platform. Behind them: a city that had been preparing for years without knowing what it was preparing for.
slides.visualDescription: Raipur station platform at dawn, December 20, 1920. Leaders in the front — Shukla, Pyarelal Singh, Dubey — flower garlands in hand. Behind them, hundreds of people pressing forward. The crowd of a city that has made itself ready.

slides.text: The train pulled in. Leaders from first class and second class compartments descended — Dadasaheb Khaparde, Dr. Munje. The crowd looked for Gandhi among them. He was not there. Then someone said: he is in the third-class compartment.
slides.visualDescription: The train arriving at Raipur. First-class passengers descending — Khaparde, Munje, important figures. The crowd searching their faces. No Gandhi. Then: a voice from the back of the crowd — he is in third class. The crowd turns and surges toward the other end.

slides.text: As captured by eyewitness Prabhu Lal Kabra: 'Gandhi, wearing a Lungi and Bandage Kurta, was standing at the door of the third-class compartment with folded hands, till then the train started moving.' The train was still in motion as Gandhi namasted the people of Chhattisgarh.
slides.visualDescription: The third-class compartment door — Gandhi in his simple dhoti and bandage kurta, hands folded in namaste, the train still slowly moving. The crowd surging forward. The image of simplicity against the backdrop of an enormous welcome. The first sight of Gandhi.

slides.text: 'Seeing Gandhi going in the third class, the public got emotional after realising his simplicity and people became convinced that only Gandhi can lead the poor and downtrodden Indian people properly.' Prabhu Lal Kabra's words carry thirty years of memory.
slides.visualDescription: Close-up of faces in the crowd at Raipur station — emotion breaking across them like a wave as they see Gandhi in third class. Some touching their hearts, some with hands over mouths. The moment of realisation: this man is genuinely like us.

slides.text: Gandhi was lodged in Barrister Thakkar's bungalow in Raipur. The Ali brothers stayed with him. The leaders of Chhattisgarh's freedom movement gathered in that bungalow — the first time so many of them had been in one room with the man they had been preparing to receive.
slides.visualDescription: Barrister Thakkar's bungalow, Raipur — a fine colonial building. Gandhi being welcomed at the entrance. Leaders of the Chhattisgarh movement crowded into the courtyard. The Ali brothers arriving. A gathering of purpose and history in one bungalow.

slides.text: That evening: the massive public meeting at the ground near Kankalipara — what would become Gandhi Chowk. Shaukat Ali spoke first. He jocularly said: 'I am like an elephant and Gandhi is like a goat.' The crowd laughed.
slides.visualDescription: The evening meeting at Kankalipara ground. Shaukat Ali at the podium — massive, commanding, speaking with humour. Gandhi seated beside him, small, still, smiling slightly. The crowd's laughter rippling outward. Wit in service of truth.

slides.text: Then Shaukat Ali continued: 'Even if I die, it will not be of any use, but Gandhi is still useful for everyone, and will remain useful even after death.' Then people understood the context of the elephant and the goat. Laughter became reverence.
slides.visualDescription: The crowd's expression shifting — from laughter to deep understanding. The philosophical weight of Shaukat Ali's words settling over 15,000 people. Gandhi still seated, unchanged. His smallness suddenly immense. The goat that outlasts the elephant.

slides.text: Gandhi spoke. He outlined the Non-Cooperation Movement. He collected contributions for the Tilak Swaraj Fund. The women of Machilabad attended openly, donating gold and silver. Muslim and Hindu women standing together for the same cause.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi at the Kankalipara podium — his voice carrying across 15,000 people in the December evening. His bag spread before him. Women pressing forward with jewelry. The Tilak Fund filling with gold, silver, and coin. Unity made tangible and material.

slides.text: The Raipur District Congress Committee was founded that same evening, with Ravi Shankar Shukla as its first secretary. A permanent organisation born from a single night's gathering. What began as a reception became the birth of an institution.
slides.visualDescription: The founding moment of the Raipur DCC — Shukla signing the papers by torchlight, Gandhi nearby, Ali brothers witnessing. The formalisation of thirty years of patient preparation. An organisation now exists where before there was only conscience.

slides.text: The next morning, December 21. Abbas Bhai's motor waits at Azad Chowk. The party assembles — Gandhi, the Ali brothers, Pt. Sharma. They are going to Dhamtari. The farmers of Kandel, who have already won, are waiting to see the man who won it for them.
slides.visualDescription: December 21 dawn. Abbas Bhai's motor at Azad Chowk, Raipur. Gandhi and the Ali brothers boarding. The road to Dhamtari stretching ahead through the winter Chhattisgarh landscape. The mission: to honour the Kandel Satyagrahis in person.

slides.text: The road to Dhamtari was filled with people. Villages on both sides of the road, people standing on rooftops, children in trees, farmers abandoning their fields to stand and catch one glimpse of the man. A nation on foot, making itself present.
slides.visualDescription: The Raipur-Dhamtari road in December 1920 — people lining both sides, standing on rooftops, children in trees. Abbas Bhai's motor moving slowly through the living corridor of humanity. Gandhi's hand raised in continuous greeting. The road as a river of people.

slides.text: A police officer tried to stop the bus driver from taking Gandhi's group. Abbas Bhai stepped forward and drove them in his own vehicle. The simple courage of an ordinary man. Later, his transport license would be cancelled. He paid the price without regret.
slides.visualDescription: Abbas Bhai confronting the police officer — not with anger but with quiet determination. Then at the wheel of his motor, driving the party forward. His face in the rear-view mirror: calm, committed. A man who knew exactly what he was risking and drove anyway.

slides.text: Makai Chowk, Dhamtari. A crowd beyond any count. The enclosure of Seth Hussain overflowing. The motor cannot push through. Omar Seth of Gurur sees what needs to be done. He lifts Gandhi onto his shoulders and carries him to the stage.
slides.visualDescription: Makai Chowk — an ocean of people. Omar Seth — large, powerful — lifting Gandhi onto his shoulders. Gandhi above the crowd, hand raised, smiling. A sea of upturned faces. One man carrying another so that thousands can see. The image of the movement itself.

slides.text: Gandhi spoke for an hour. He praised Babu Chhotelal Srivastava by name — the man who had led the Kandel Satyagraha with quiet determination. For Srivastava, hearing his name from Gandhi's lips before 15,000 people was the defining moment of his life.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi at the Dhamtari podium, pointing toward Babu Chhotelal Srivastava in the crowd. Srivastava's face: the overwhelming emotion of being honoured by the person whose name won your battle. The crowd turning to see him. A hero named.

slides.text: Bajirao Kridatta presented Rs 501 to Gandhi in the name of the Tilak Swaraj Fund. More than 500 activists committed to attend the Nagpur Congress session. The movement was not just witnessed — it was joined.
slides.visualDescription: The contribution at Dhamtari — Bajirao Kridatta presenting a bag of Rs 501 to Gandhi. 500 raised hands committing to Nagpur. The meeting as recruitment, as commitment, as formal joining of the national movement. Dhamtari choosing its side.

slides.text: Shaukat Ali and Muhammad Ali addressed the Muslim gathering at Yateemkhana in Dhamtari, December 21. The Khilafat message given in the same town where the Kandel Satyagraha had just succeeded. Two movements meeting in one geography.
slides.visualDescription: Yateemkhana, Dhamtari — a Muslim community gathering. Shaukat Ali speaking — his large frame at the podium, his voice powerful. The Khilafat Movement addressing its community in the same town as the Kandel Satyagraha. Convergence of national causes.

slides.text: The evening meeting back in Raipur — the massive gathering at Kankalipara near the Anand Samaj library. A drama had played the night before on this same stage. Now it holds Gandhi, the Ali brothers, 15,000 people, and the birth of an organisation.
slides.visualDescription: Kankalipara ground, evening of December 21. The stage that hosted a drama the night before now hosting Gandhi. 15,000 people under the stars. The contrast: yesterday's drama, tonight's history. The same ground, a different kind of theatre.

slides.text: After the meeting, those with reverence took bricks from the stage as mementos. The stage itself was dismantled piece by piece out of pure devotion. What was built to hold Gandhi's meeting was taken apart by the people who loved him.
slides.visualDescription: After the meeting — people reverently taking bricks from the stage. Hands reaching, faces solemn and joyful. The stage disappearing into the crowd, distributed among thousands as sacred objects. The material of Gandhi's presence made holy by touch.

slides.text: Gandhi visited the Jaitasava monastery that evening. A moment of spiritual stillness inside the motion of the political movement. The meeting of Gandhian activism and the religious life of Chhattisgarh — both present, both real.
slides.visualDescription: The Jaitasava monastery — ancient, quiet, sacred. Gandhi entering barefoot, head bowed. The monks receiving him. The activist entering a space of contemplation. Politics and spirituality meeting in a monastery courtyard. A man of action in a place of prayer.

slides.text: December 22, 1920. Gandhi departs from Raipur station for Nagpur. His three days in Chhattisgarh are over. But in those three days, a Satyagraha was honoured, a Congress committee was founded, and 15,000 people were changed.
slides.visualDescription: Raipur station, December 22 morning. Gandhi at the platform, bag in hand, the Ali brothers beside him. Shukla, Sharma, Srivastava seeing them off. The train departing slowly. The crowd on the platform watching until the last carriage disappears.

slides.text: What did Pt. Sundarlal Sharma's invitation achieve? A Satyagraha won, a DCC founded, 500 people committed to Nagpur, the Tilak Fund enriched, and the name of Gandhi now spoken in every village of Chhattisgarh. Everything. The invitation achieved everything.
slides.visualDescription: The cascading consequences of the invitation: the Kandel victory, the DCC founding, the Nagpur commitments, the Tilak Fund, and the name Gandhi spreading across Chhattisgarh like a wave. Sharma's simple journey to Calcutta made visible in its full consequence.

slides.text: Pt. Sundarlal Sharma — who went to Calcutta alone, found Gandhi, told him about Kandel, and brought him to Raipur — is the unacknowledged architect of this entire moment. Without his journey, Gandhi would have gone to Nagpur without stopping.
slides.visualDescription: Pt. Sundarlal Sharma alone at Calcutta station, the city behind him — the moment before he found Gandhi. His journey. His decision. His action. The pivot of history in the form of one man's railway ticket. The bridge that made the meeting possible.

slides.text: The Khilafat and Non-Cooperation movements, traveling together on this journey, represented Gandhi's greatest political achievement: the unity of Hindu and Muslim Indians against colonial rule. In Chhattisgarh, this unity was not abstract — it was a room, a motor, a stage.
slides.visualDescription: The unity of the visit made concrete — Gandhi and Ali brothers in one motor, Hindu and Muslim women donating together, Shukla and Asgar Ali standing at the same podium. Unity not as principle but as practice, as daily lived reality in December 1920.

slides.text: The Tilak Swaraj Fund collected in those three days — cash, gold rings, silver jewelry — was the material expression of a people's commitment. Not a donation to a cause, but a conversion of personal value into collective purpose.
slides.visualDescription: The Tilak Swaraj Fund in close-up — gold rings, silver bracelets, coins of all denominations piled together. Each object was someone's most precious thing. Each one given willingly. The material form of commitment. Personal sacrifice made collective.

slides.text: Gandhi on the train to Nagpur. Sharma beside him. The Ali brothers in the next compartment. Outside: the forests and fields of Chhattisgarh passing. Behind them: a changed province. Ahead: the Nagpur session that will formally launch Non-Cooperation.
slides.visualDescription: The Nagpur-bound train moving through Chhattisgarh's landscape. Inside: Gandhi looking out the window, thoughtful. The land passing — its villages, its forests, its rivers. Behind the train: a changed province. Ahead: the next chapter of the freedom struggle.

slides.text: The Nagpur Congress session of December 26, 1920 would pass the Non-Cooperation resolution. Five hundred representatives from Dhamtari would be there. Chhattisgarh would not merely observe the national movement — it would vote for it.
slides.visualDescription: The Nagpur Congress session — a vast gathering of delegates from across India. Among them: 500 from Dhamtari, Chhattisgarh. The Non-Cooperation resolution being put to vote. Chhattisgarh's hands raised among thousands. The region casting its vote for freedom.

slides.text: After the Nagpur session, the Non-Cooperation Movement would change every village in Chhattisgarh. Lawyers would leave their practices. Titles would be surrendered. Schools would be established. Khadi would be worn. The invitation had set all of this in motion.
slides.visualDescription: A cascade of consequences: lawyers closing their offices, titles being surrendered, national schools opening, charkhas spinning, khadi being worn. All of this flowing from one journey — Sharma's invitation, Gandhi's acceptance, three days in Chhattisgarh.

slides.text: This was the first visit. Gandhi came as Mohandas — the lawyer, the organiser, the man of principle. He left having been transformed into something more in the eyes of Chhattisgarh: the proof that one person's presence could change everything.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi on the train — his profile in the window, the December light on his face. He is still Mohandas. But in the eyes of 15,000 people in Raipur and Dhamtari, something has shifted. The man and the myth beginning to merge. The first visit complete.

slides.text: Pt. Sundarlal Sharma — the bridge between Gandhi and Chhattisgarh — would continue his work through the 1920s and into the 1930s. When Gandhi returned in 1933 as The Mahatma, he would say of Sharma: 'You are even my Guru in the salvation of Harijans.'
slides.visualDescription: Pt. Sundarlal Sharma in contemplation — a man whose life's work was about to be acknowledged by the person he admired most. Gandhi's future words visible as text: Harijan Uddhar mein aap mere bhi guru hain. A preview of the recognition thirteen years away.

slides.text: The invitation was extended by Pt. Sundarlal Sharma. It was accepted by Gandhi. It was received by 15,000 people in Raipur, 15,000 in Dhamtari, and every village and forest and field between them that heard the name Gandhi spoken afterward.
slides.visualDescription: The invitation completed — its ripples spreading outward from Raipur across the map of Chhattisgarh. Each village, each field, each river touched by the wave that began with one man's train ticket from Chhattisgarh to Calcutta and back again.

slides.text: Mohandas has arrived. What he ignited next would last for decades. Next: Episode 8 — Mohandas Arrives.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi's face at the train window — the platform of Raipur in 1920 visible, the crowd surging forward, his hands folded in namaste. The first sight that 15,000 people would carry in their hearts forever. Title card: Episode 8 — Mohandas Arrives.
